replication_target_quote: One perspective on embodiment proposes that bodily states exert direct, context-free effects on psychological states, as in the research on “power poses.”
outcome_quote: In Study 1, expansive and constrictive poses influenced power only when held in an interpersonal context, which provides action-relevant meaning to these poses as dominance and submissiveness. In Study 2, poses had no effect on power when roles provided more important information about potential action
review_note: Independent conceptual boundary test of original pose-to-power experience: Study 1 shows power effect only with interpersonal context; Study 2 shows no pose effect when role cues dominate. original_title: Threatened egotism, narcissism, self-esteem, and direct and displaced aggression: does self-love or self-hate lead to violence?
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effect_name: Narcissism plus insult increases aggression
effect_claim: People higher in narcissism responded to a personal insult with more direct aggression against the insulter.
effect_claim_quote: The combination of narcissism and insult led to exceptionally high levels of aggression toward the source of the insult.
replication_title: Sound the Alarm: The Effect of Narcissism on Retaliatory Aggression Is Moderated by dACC Reactivity to Rejection
replication_target_quote: This study tested the hypothesis that narcissism would only predict greater retaliatory aggression in response to social rejection when the dACC was recruited by the threat.
outcome_quote: When narcissists displayed greater dACC activation during rejection, they behaved aggressively. But there was only a weak or nonsignificant relation between narcissism and aggression among participants with a blunted dACC response.
review_note: Independent conceptual retest and mechanistic extension of the threatened-egotism aggression effect: social rejection replaces direct interpersonal insult; aggression is an aversive noise blast directed at a rejecter. N=30. The narcissism–aggression association was conditional on dACC activation, so mixed for the broad original claim. University of Kentucky publication record lists print year 2016; OpenAlex online publication 2015. Later OpenAlex primary field Psychology.

original_title: Shared neural mechanisms underlying social warmth and physical warmth
effect_name: Physical warmth increases feelings of social connection
effect_claim: Holding a warm pack increased participants’ reported feelings of social connection compared with holding a neutral object.
effect_claim_quote: more connected after holding the warm pack (compared with the ball)
replication_target_quote: Replicating previous research, holding a warm (vs. a cold or neutral) object increased feelings of social connection.
outcome_quote: Replicating previous research, holding a warm (vs. a cold or neutral) object increased feelings of social connection.
review_note: Corrected the queue’s mismatched Williams and Bargh (2008) original. The later full paper explicitly identifies Inagaki and Eisenberger (2013) as the prior study in which holding a warm pack increased feelings of social connection. The 2013 fMRI participants and the later double-blind naltrexone/placebo crossover group of 31 are distinct; this pair is limited to the warm-object self-reported connection effect, not the neural overlap or opioid extension.
replication_title: Blocking opioids attenuates physical warmth-induced feelings of social connection.

original_title: Response-restriction analysis: I. Assessment of activity preferences
effect_name: Response restriction yields fuller preference assessment than free operant observation
effect_claim: Response restriction produced more differentiated and complete information about activity preferences than an extended free operant assessment in adults with developmental disabilities.
effect_claim_quote: the RR assessment yielded (a) more differentiated patterns of preference and (b) more complete information about engagement with all of the target activities
replication_target_quote: We replicated the response‐restriction (RR) preference assessment and compared results in terms of preference hierarchies to those from free‐operant and multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO) formats with six children with autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
outcome_quote: Complete hierarchies were produced in four of 18 assessments and with MSWO and RR formats only.
review_note: Corrected the queue’s unrelated Hanley et al. (2014) DOI: the later Wiley article cites Hanley et al. (2003), Response-restriction analysis: I, as the method being replicated. Original sample was three adults with developmental disabilities; later sample was six children with autism. Both found RR could produce a fuller preference hierarchy than free operant, but only four of eighteen later assessments produced complete hierarchies, and MSWO also succeeded; coded mixed to preserve that limit.
replication_title: A replication of the response‐restriction preference assessment

original_title: Altercentric interference in level 1 visual perspective taking reflects the ascription of mental states, not submentalizing
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
effect_name: Visual access gates altercentric interference in the goggles task
effect_claim: Participants’ own-perspective response times showed altercentric interference when an avatar’s goggles were believed transparent, but not when they were believed opaque.
effect_claim_quote: Altercentric interference was observed when participants judged their own perspective on stimuli involving an avatar wearing goggles that participants believed to be transparent but not when they believed the goggles to be opaque.
replication_target_quote: In Study 2, we conducted a conceptual replication of what we thought was the most convincing finding in support of the implicit mentalizing position to date
outcome_quote: Although we failed to find evidence of altercentric interference in response times, participants' accuracy reflected the possibility of interference from others' perspectives.
review_note: Corrected the queue’s Kovács et al. (2010) mismatch. The later paper expressly identifies Furlanetto et al. (2016), DOI 10.1037/xhp0000138, as Study 2’s goggles-paradigm original. Its new online MTurk sample had 34 analyzed adults versus the original lab sample of 17. Original response-time interference was not replicated, but the later error-rate pattern supported visual-access-gated interference; hence mixed. Study 1 tests a separate avatar-versus-arrow effect and is not this pair.
replication_title: Does altercentric interference rely on mentalizing?: Results from two level-1 perspective-taking tasks

original_title: Does Language Shape Thought?: Mandarin and English Speakers' Conceptions of Time
effect_name: Mandarin vertical time representation
effect_claim: Mandarin speakers showed a stronger vertical spatial representation of time than English speakers, even when tested in English.
effect_claim_quote: Mandarin speakers tended to think about time vertically even when they were thinking for English
replication_title: Mental Representations of Time in English Monolinguals, Mandarin Monolinguals, and Mandarin–English Bilinguals
replication_target_quote: This study recruited English monolinguals, Mandarin monolinguals, and Mandarin-English (ME) bilinguals to examine whether native English and native Mandarin speakers think about time differently and whether the acquisition of L2 English could reshape native Mandarin speakers' mental representations of temporal sequence.
outcome_quote: Results add to previous studies by confirming that native English and native Mandarin speakers do think about time differently, and the significant crosslinguistic discrepancy primarily lies in the vertical representations of time flow.
review_note: Independent conceptual retest with two reaction-time experiments; replicates the crosslinguistic vertical-time difference. It does not reproduce Boroditsky’s exact spatial-priming task or isolate testing in English; its separate L2-acquisition hypothesis failed. Full text explicitly says it replicates previous English/Mandarin differences and cites Boroditsky 2001. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

original_title: Does Language Shape Thought?: Mandarin and English Speakers' Conceptions of Time
effect_name: Mandarin vertical time representation
effect_claim: Mandarin speakers showed a stronger vertical spatial representation of time than English speakers, even when tested in English.
effect_claim_quote: Mandarin speakers tended to think about time vertically even when they were thinking for English
replication_title: English and Mandarin speakers’ mental representations of time: Some new evidence about the language-thought relationship
replication_target_quote: Focusing on these controversial issues, the present study examines and refines the findings from previous work with some new evidence.
outcome_quote: Converging results yielded from the two experiments demonstrate that most Mandarin speakers (approximately 80%) may be identical to English speakers with regard to their salient horizontal bias for temporal cognition. Only approximately 20% of Mandarin speakers, who overwhelmingly rely on the vertical axis to reason about time, may differ from English speakers.
review_note: Independent conceptual retest with card arrangement and video-order judgments in English and Mandarin speakers. A vertical-thinking subgroup appeared, but about 80% of Mandarin speakers showed the same salient horizontal bias as English speakers. Published in 2016 journal volume, online January 2017. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

replication_target_quote: We report on a pre-registered, multi-lab replication of one version of the ACE.
outcome_quote: The results show that none of the 18 labs involved in the study observed a reliable ACE, and that the meta-analytic estimate of the size of the ACE was essentially zero.
review_note: 18 laboratory samples tested one version of Glenberg and Kaschak (2002)’s action-sentence compatibility effect, including original authors as coauthors. replication_target_quote: Here, we conducted a replication of the original study, in which we tested 14- to 16-month-olds using a familiarization procedure with three-dimensional animated video stimuli.
outcome_quote: In contrast with the original results, only 16 out of 32 infants (50%) in our study reached for the helper; thus, we were not able to replicate the findings.
review_note: The later study explicitly names Hamlin et al. (2007), uses the original hill-helper/hinderer choice paradigm, and tests a distinct 14–16-month-old cohort of 32 infants. review_note: Same-author 2019 study explicitly replicates Kievit et al. (2017) with the same vocabulary/reasoning measures and model comparison in a distinct younger cohort (227 children aged 6–8 versus original adolescents and young adults aged 14–25). effect_claim_quote: forcing subjects to decide quickly increases contributions, whereas instructing them to reflect and forcing them to decide slowly decreases contributions.
replication_target_quote: This Registered Replication Report (RRR) assessed the size and variability of the effect of time pressure on cooperative decisions by combining 21 separate, preregistered replications of the critical conditions from Study 7 of the original article (Rand et al., 2012).
outcome_quote: In combination, the results of the intent-to-treat analysis and the compliant-only analysis are consistent with the presence of selection biases and the absence of a causal effect of time pressure on cooperation.
review_note: 21 independent preregistered laboratory samples directly retested the critical Study 7 time-pressure versus forced-delay conditions. The primary intent-to-treat estimate was -0.37 percentage points versus +8.6 in the original; the positive compliant-only result was consistent with selection bias, not a causal effect. Scope is the randomized causal time-pressure claim, a separate effect from the intuition-prime effect already curated.
replication_title: Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene, and Nowak (2012)

original_title: Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis.
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effect_name: Facial feedback changes cartoon humor ratings
effect_claim: Facilitating a smile increases rated cartoon humor compared with inhibiting a smile.
effect_claim_quote: Subjects reported more intense humor responses when cartoons were presented under facilitating conditions than under inhibiting conditions
replication_target_quote: To test the hypothesis, we replicated the facial-feedback experiment in 2 conditions: one with a video-camera and one without it.
outcome_quote: The results revealed a significant facial-feedback effect in the absence of a camera, which was eliminated in the camera's presence.
review_note: Independent participant sample repeated the pen-in-mouth cartoon rating task. The original no-camera protocol produced a significant effect, while an added camera condition did not. Mixed coding records the protocol moderator; the exact original context succeeded. The later authors replaced cartoons with pretested Hebrew cartoons.
replication_title: When both the original study and its failed replication are correct: Feeling observed eliminates the facial-feedback effect.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

original_title: Red, rank, and romance in women viewing men.
effect_name: Red increases perceived male attractiveness
effect_claim: A red background or red clothing increases women’s ratings of men’s attractiveness.
effect_claim_quote: women perceive men to be more attractive and sexually desirable when seen on a red background and in red clothing
replication_target_quote: The present article reports the results of a meta-analysis of nine student replication projects of Elliot et al.’s (2010) findings from Experiment 3, that women were more attracted to photographs of men with red borders (total n = 640).
outcome_quote: Results of this meta-analysis showed no effect of red on attractiveness ratings for either perceived attractiveness (mean ratings difference = –0.07, 95% CI [–0.31, 0.16]) or sexual attractiveness (mean ratings difference = –0.06, 95% CI [–0.36, 0.24]); this null result held with and without Elliot et al.’s (2010) data included in analyses.
review_note: Nine independent student replication projects (n=640) directly retested Experiment 3 red-border photographs, with expert protocol review and preregistration before collection. Both attractiveness outcomes were null in the pooled analysis. The original broad effect also included red clothing; this retest addresses its red-border component.
replication_title: A Demonstration of the Collaborative Replication and Education Project: Replication Attempts of the Red-Romance Effect

original_title: Class-Wide Function-Related Intervention Teams: Effects of Group Contingency Programs in Urban Classrooms
effect_name: CW FIT and on task behavior
effect_claim: Class Wide Function related Intervention Teams increases pupils’ on task behavior.
effect_claim_quote: Group on-task data improved during CW-FIT over baseline levels.
replication_target_quote: The present study examined the effects of the Class-Wide Function-Related Intervention Team (CW-FIT) program, a group contingency intervention addressing the on-task and disruptive behavior of students with or at risk for emotional behavior disorders (EBD).
outcome_quote: Results confirmed that CW-FIT can be used to increase on-task behavior and reduce disruptive behavior of students with or at risk for EBD.
review_note: New multisite six-month trial in 21 elementary schools, 155 teachers and 324 students retested CW-FIT engagement benefit in distinct school cohorts, expanding the original six classrooms/107 students. Same intervention and on-task direct-observation endpoint; the later publisher calls it a replication trial.
replication_title: Classroom Management That Works: A Replication Trial of the CW-FIT Program

original_title: Cognitive principles of multimedia learning: The role of modality and contiguity.
effect_name: Auditory narration improves multimedia learning over on-screen text
effect_claim: Students learned more when verbal material was spoken rather than displayed as on-screen text alongside visual material.
effect_claim_quote: students learned better when verbal input was presented auditorily as speech rather than visually as text.
replication_target_quote: Adopting a German translation of the learning materials used by Moreno and Mayer (1999) , we failed to detect a modality effect for sequential text-picture-presentation in Experiment 1.
outcome_quote: In Experiment 2, a modality effect was expected for simultaneous presentation of the same texts and pictures, yet again remained absent.
review_note: Two new experiments translated Moreno and Mayer (1999) learning materials into German and compared auditory narration with written text; neither sequential nor simultaneous design detected the original modality advantage. Distinct participants. This is a separate 2011 paper from Tabbers/van der Spoel DOI a000047.
replication_title: On the Robustness of the Modality Effect: Attempting to Replicate a Basic Finding

original_title: Social evaluation by preverbal infants
effect_name: Infants prefer helpers to hinderers
effect_claim: Infants preferred helping agents over hindering agents when choosing between them.
effect_claim_quote: infants prefer an individual who helps another to one who hinders another
replication_target_quote: We present a preregistered, multi-laboratory, standardized study aimed at replicating infants' preference for Helpers over Hinderers.
outcome_quote: Overall, 49.34% of infants preferred Helpers over Hinderers in the social condition, and 55.85% preferred characters who pushed up, versus down, an inanimate object in the nonsocial condition; neither proportion differed from chance or from each other.
review_note: ManyBabies coordinated retest of the exact 2007 hill-helper/hinderer preference, with 1,018 tested infants, 567 included (5.5–10.5 months) from 37 independent labs across five continents. It matched the original age range and found no helper preference. The DOI was first published online in November 2024 although print issue is 2025. FLoRA's older mixed/positive quote conflicts with the final preregistered main result in the publisher paper; the 2025 publisher correction (doi:10.1111/desc.70029) explicitly leaves study conclusions unchanged. Outcome here follows the final primary result.
replication_title: Infants’ Social Evaluation of Helpers and Hinderers: A Large‐Scale, Multi‐Lab, Coordinated Replication Study

original_title: Measuring the Suicidal Mind
effect_name: Suicide-IAT predicts future attempts
effect_claim: Stronger implicit self–death association predicts a new suicide attempt within six months beyond known risk factors.
effect_claim_quote: the implicit association of death/suicide with self was associated with an approximately 6-fold increase in the odds of making a suicide attempt in the next 6 months, exceeding the predictive validity of known risk factors
replication_target_quote: We report the first direct and independent replication of this promising finding.
outcome_quote: As in the original study, however, the S-IAT predicted suicide attempts within the 6-month follow-up period beyond well-known predictors.
review_note: Independent prospective sample of 165 French psychiatric-unit patients, reassessed at six months, directly retested Nock et al. (2010). The future-attempt prediction reproduced beyond known predictors (85% correctly classified). The baseline attempted-versus-other-admission comparison did not reproduce, but this new effect row is scoped solely to prospective prediction. Published online 2019, print 2020. FLoRA's paper-level mixed label covers a separate baseline discrimination result that failed; this record captures only the preregistered future-attempt prediction effect, for which the SAGE abstract says the original result reproduced.
replication_title: Forecasting a Fatal Decision: Direct Replication of the Predictive Validity of the Suicide–Implicit Association Test

effect_name: Mere exposure increases liking
effect_claim: Repeated exposure to nonsense words increases positive meaning ratings.
effect_claim_quote: the effect of experimentally manipulated frequency of exposure upon the affective connotation of nonsense words and symbols
original_title: Attitudinal effects of mere exposure
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Trait and state anxiety reduce the mere exposure effect
replication_target_quote: The mere exposure effect refers to an affective preference elicited by exposure to previously unfamiliar items.
outcome_quote: In both experiments, greater anxiety was associated with a reduced mere exposure effect.
review_note: Independent close conceptual retest with novel nonwords, the original kind of stimulus, and affective preference. Higher trait or state anxiety reduced the effect, so the exposure-to-liking pattern is conditional. The state-anxiety manipulation was ineffective; the reported moderation is correlational. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Does mere exposure enhance positive evaluation, independent of stimulus recognition? A replication study in Japan and the USA1
replication_target_quote: In order to examine whether the mere exposure effect, the finding that exposure to a stimulus enhances a positive evaluation of it, occurs in Japan as well as in the USA, a test was carried out using a novel auditory stimulus.
outcome_quote: The mere exposure effect was found in both cultures. Further, it resulted from only exposure frequency, not recognition.
review_note: Independent direct replication with unfamiliar Tagalog utterances rather than printed nonsense words. Repeated auditory exposure increased liking in Japanese and American samples; recognition did not explain it. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

effect_name: Gain versus loss framing changes risk choice
effect_claim: Equivalent disease outcomes framed as lives saved or lost produce different risky choices.
effect_claim_quote: Reversals of preference are demonstrated in choices regarding monetary outcomes, both hypothetical and real, and in questions pertaining to the loss of human lives.
original_title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
replication_title: The Dark Triad trait of psychopathy and message framing predict risky decision‐making during the COVID ‐19 pandemic
replication_target_quote: The effects of framing on risky decision-making have been studied extensively in research using Kahneman and Tversky's (1981) hypothetical scenario about a contagious Asian disease.
outcome_quote: People were more risk-averse in the loss condition of the current study compared to the benchmark established by Tversky and Kahneman (1981).
review_note: Independent conceptual retest of disease-policy gain/loss messages in a real COVID-19 setting, US adults N=294. Framing affected choices but loss-framed respondents were more risk averse than the classic benchmark, so mixed for the original direction and magnitude. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

replication_title: To save or lose? A cross‐national examination of the disease risk framing effect and the influence of collectivism
replication_target_quote: we examined the robustness of Tversky and Kahneman's (1981) framing effect within each country using a variation of the classic Asian Disease Scenario.
outcome_quote: was replicated in 100% of the countries examined
review_note: Independent large cross-national retest of the classic Asian Disease choice framing, N=102,830 across 49 countries. The gain-frame preference for the safe option relative to the loss frame recurred everywhere studied. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

effect_claim: Equivalent disease outcomes framed as lives saved or lost produce different risky choices.
effect_claim_quote: Reversals of preference are demonstrated in choices regarding monetary outcomes, both hypothetical and real, and in questions pertaining to the loss of human lives.
original_title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
replication_title: The Influence of Trait Emotion and Spatial Distance on Risky Choice Under the Framework of Gain and Loss
replication_target_quote: the dependent variable is the choice of the rescue plan for the classic "Asian disease" problem.
outcome_quote: Distant spatial distance lead individuals to increase their preference for risk-seeking under the gain frame, which leads to the disappearance of the framing effect.
review_note: Independent two-study direct use of classic Asian Disease rescue-plan choices. Gain/loss framing appeared in ordinary/proximal conditions but disappeared at far spatial distance. Mixed for context-independent choice reversal. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

effect_name: Gain versus loss framing changes risk choice

replication_title: How Prone are Bulgarians to Heuristics and Biases? Implications for Studying Rationality across Cultures
replication_target_quote: Here, we explored whether effects predicted by prospect theory, such as the framing effect, would be observed in a sample of 312 Bulgarian students.
outcome_quote: Most notably, we failed to reproduce the framing effect in the famous Asian Disease problem, using a rating response format.
review_note: Independent Bulgarian sample, N=312. This is a format-dependent failure: respondents rated options rather than making the original binary choice. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

original_title: Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority
effect_name: Unanimous majorities shift visual line judgments
effect_claim: A unanimous majority giving the wrong line-length judgment can shift a minority participant toward that answer.
effect_claim_quote: The unanimously wrong majority produced a marked and significant distortion in the reported estimates.
replication_target_quote: In the present study, we tried to replicate a classic Asch effect in the cultural context of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to explore the potential impact of group similarity on conformity.
outcome_quote: In line with past research, the results revealed a clear-cut and powerful "Asch effect" wherein participants followed the majority in 35.4% of critical trials.
review_note: Independent Bosnian student sample (N=95) performed the classic line judgment task with five confederates; the wrong-majority conformity rate was 35.4% of critical trials, close to Asch’s original. In-group versus out-group identity moderated the effect. Original result excerpt is from a facsimile of Asch’s 1956 monograph, p. 12.
replication_title: Replication of the "Asch effect" in Bosnia and Herzegovin

original_title: The effects of smiling on perceived age defy belief
effect_name: Smiling increases estimated facial age
effect_claim: Smiling faces are estimated as older than neutral faces.
effect_claim_quote: smiling faces were perceived as older than neutral faces.
replication_target_quote: Specifically, we aimed to replicate Ganel and Goodale's study using segregated sets of Japanese and Swedish facial stimuli, and including Japanese and Swedish participants in groups asked to estimate the age of either Japanese or Swedish faces (two groups of participants × two groups of stimuli; four groups total).
outcome_quote: Our multiverse analytical approach consistently showed that the participants evaluated smiling faces as older in direct evaluations, regardless of the facial stimuli culture or their nationality, although they believed that smiling makes people look younger.
review_note: Registered independent cross-cultural replication used new Japanese and Swedish participants and face stimuli in a four-group design. Smiling faces were estimated as older across participant and stimulus cultures, with contrary beliefs preserved. Original 2017 online publication appeared in a 2018 print issue; existing curated metadata use 2017. Earlier manuscript version: https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/dtx6j. It reports this same replication sample and is linked here, counted once.
replication_title: Age of smile: a cross-cultural replication report of Ganel and Goodale (2018)

original_title: Coming Out in the Classroom... An Occupational Hazard?: The Influence of Sexual Orientation on Teacher Credibility and Perceived Student Learning
effect_name: Instructor sexual orientation credibility bias
effect_claim: Students rate a male instructor as less credible when he identifies as gay than when he identifies as straight.
effect_claim_quote: Findings indicate that students perceive a gay teacher as significantly less credible than a straight teacher.
replication_target_quote: Our purpose was to see if the original findings—that students perceive gay teachers as less credible and that they learn less than from a straight teacher—could be replicated in a sample of students from a different location and after more than 15 years from the original study.
outcome_quote: Employing a quasi-experimental methodology, we did not find the same result as they did: gay instructors were not rated lower in credibility and learning by the students in our sample.
review_note: Boren and McPherson’s independent student sample at a different location repeated the instructor sexual-orientation disclosure contrast more than 15 years after Russ et al. (2002). Their author-hosted abstract reports no lower gay-instructor credibility or perceived learning. Later OpenAlex primary field Psychology; FORRT FLoRA also codes this exact later DOI failed.
replication_title: Is Coming Out in the Classroom Still an Occupational Hazard? A Replication of Russ, Simonds, and Hunt (2002)

original_title: Can you connect with me now? How the presence of mobile communication technology influences face-to-face conversation quality
original_journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
effect_name: Phone presence reduces conversation quality
effect_claim: A visible mobile phone during face-to-face conversation lowers perceived relationship quality between strangers.
effect_claim_quote: In both, we found evidence they can have negative effects on closeness, connection, and conversation quality.
replication_target_quote: The purpose of the present research is twofold: (1) closely replicate this article's findings, and (2) examine whether there may be an impact of the mere presence of a phone on creativity, whether at a group- or an individual- level.
outcome_quote: In both studies, we failed to replicate the original results on relationship quality.
review_note: Corrected original to Przybylski and Weinstein (2013) DOI 10.1177/0265407512453827; the queue’s cited mind-wandering original was unrelated. Two independent experiments with 356 participants and 136 groups repeated phone-versus-notebook conversations among strangers and found no relationship-quality reduction. Later full PLOS paper explicitly identifies original Study 1 as the target. Original paper was online 2012, print 2013.
replication_title: How bad is the mere presence of a phone? A replication of Przybylski and Weinstein (2013) and an extension to creativity

replication_title: Social contagion of autobiographical memories.

review_note: Independent conceptual retest with personal autobiographical events; 30% recalled a confederate-suggested detail. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

review_note: Independent retest in 48 preschoolers with alternative film versions; most transferred errors persisted in private recall. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

replication_target_quote: In this study we used the social contagion paradigm to investigate

review_note: Independent autobiographical-memory retest; contagion occurred in 20%, though natural variation was more frequent. OpenAlex primary Psychology.

replication_title: Robustness of the rule‐learning effect in 7‐month‐old infants: A close, multicenter replication of Marcus et al. (1999)
replication_target_quote: We conducted a close replication of the seminal work by Marcus and colleagues from 1999

original_title: Rumination on unwanted intrusive thoughts affects the urge to neutralize in nonclinical individuals
original_authors: Wahl, van den Hout, and Lieb
original_journal: Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
effect_name: Rumination on intrusive thoughts maintains neutralizing urge

replication_title: Effects of rumination on unwanted intrusive thoughts: A replication and extension

original_title: The substitutability of physical and social warmth in daily life

original_title: Neuromodulation of group prejudice and religious belief
effect_name: pMFC downregulation reduces positive religious belief after death reminder

review_note: Independent preregistered TMS experiment added active control-site stimulation and neutral writing. Planned death-reminder positive-belief contrast replicated p=.038. Group-bias result failed, outside this effect.

original_title: Teaching Academic Vocabulary to Sixth-Grade Students With Disabilities
effect_name: CHAAOS improves taught academic vocabulary
effect_claim: CHAAOS classroom instruction improves knowledge of taught academic vocabulary versus ordinary instruction.
effect_claim_quote: ANCOVAs (with each cycle’s pretest and intelligence quotient as covariates) were conducted on taught vocabulary, all of which favored the treatment condition with effect sizes ranging .6 to .7 per cycle.

Generalized reading comprehension remained null. Correct original is 2019 DOI, not 2020 follow-up of original cohort.
replication_title: Improving Academic Vocabulary for Adolescent Students With Disabilities: A Replication Study

original_title: The affect heuristic in judgments of risks and benefits
effect_name: Risk information inversely shifts benefit judgments
effect_claim: Increasing perceived risk of a technology through information lowers perceived benefit.
effect_claim_quote: Study 2 tested and confirmed the hypothesis that providing information designed to alter the favorability of one's overall affective evaluation of an item (say nuclear power) would systematically change the risk and benefit judgments for that item.
replication_target_quote: Finucane et al. causally demonstrated that increasing risks of a hazard leads people to judge its benefits as lower.
outcome_quote: In two well-powered studies, using a more stringent analytic strategy, we replicated the original finding.
review_note: Two new US/UK online samples combined N=1552 closely retested Finucane Study 2 with original vignettes. Narrow risk-information-to-benefit result replicated. Low-benefit information failed to shift risk judgments, so success does not extend to every reciprocal manipulation or to affect mediation.
replication_title: Risky Therefore Not Beneficial: Replication and Extension of Finucane et al.’s (2000) Affect Heuristic Experiment

original_title: Bullseye! How Power Improves Motor Performance
effect_name: High-power priming improves golf putting
effect_claim: Priming high power improves golf-putting performance compared with neutral recall.
effect_claim_quote: Experiment 1 found that individuals primed with high-power outperformed control participants on a golf-putting task.
replication_target_quote: We conducted two high-powered direct replications of the effects of power on golf
outcome_quote: Overall, we found little to no effect of power on motor skill (d = 0.09, 95% CI[-0.07, 0.22], n = 603).
review_note: Two independent high-powered direct golf replications plus three conceptual tests did not reproduce the large original motor benefit. Aggregate d=.09, CI spans zero; small benefit remains possible.

replication_target_quote: Experiments 1 and 2 (Ns = 69 and 104) are direct replications of Lichtenfeld, Maier, Elliot, and Pekrun (2009).

effect_claim: Men are more likely than women to accept a stranger’s sexual invitation, while receptivity to a date invitation is similar.
effect_claim_quote: The great majority of men were willing to have a sexual liaison with the women who approached them. Women were not. Not one woman agreed to a sexual liaison.
replication_target_quote: Clark and Hatfield (1989) found that men were more willing than women to accept casual sexual invitations, whereas no significant gender differences were observed in responses to propositions for non-committal social activities.
outcome_quote: In both studies, men more readily than women accepted a sexual invitation from a stranger of the opposite gender. In contrast to the original study, the gender difference was independent of the type of proposition.
review_note: Two new preregistered naturalistic field samples total N=240 reproduce sex difference for sexual offers but not interaction with proposition type. Original 1989 publisher DOI is canonical despite 2008 online digitization.
replication_title: Gender differences in receptivity to sexual invitations: two naturalistic replication studies

effect_claim: After eating pretzels to induce thirst, adults predict preferring water over pretzels tomorrow, whereas baseline adults do not.
effect_claim_quote: In Study 2, we obtained baseline preferences from adults (N = 35) and confirmed that, prior to consuming pretzels, people do not anticipate wanting water more than pretzels the next day.
replication_target_quote: One study to date has examined adults' induced episodic foresight and found that adults' (like children's) preferences for the future are related to their current state such that they predicted wanting water (vs. pretzels) in the future when experiencing a current state of thirst [1].
outcome_quote: Partially replicating Kramer et al. [1], we found that a minority of adults preferred pretzels (vs. water) when experiencing a current state of thirst. However, in contrast to their findings, our results showed that when thirst was not induced, a minority of adults also preferred pretzels for tomorrow.
review_note: Independent laboratory n198 and lecture n63 adult samples. Both show water preferred after thirst induction, but crucial induced-versus-uninduced difference from Kramer is absent; code mixed only for joint induced and baseline scope.
replication_title: “These pretzels are making me thirsty” so I’ll have water tomorrow: A partial replication and extension of adults’ induced-state episodic foresight

original_title: Vividness of the Future Self Predicts Delinquency
effect_name: Letter to distant future self reduces delinquent choices

replication_target_quote: In two pre-registered, direct replication studies, we tested a subtle manipulation, that is, writing a letter to one's future self, in order to reduce delinquent decisions (van Gelder et al., 2013, Study 1) and risky investments (Monroe et al., 2017, Study 1).
outcome_quote: In the replication study, the three-months and 20-years conditions did not differ significantly (t(312) = 1.49, p = .137, d = 0.17, 90% CI [-0.02, 0.35], 95% CI [-0.05, 0.39], n = 314).

review_note: Independent authors and new online participant sample n=314 replicated van Gelder et al. 2013 Study 1 letter-writing contrast. Original effect d=0.39, p=.047; replication same-direction but smaller d=0.17, p=.137, so code failed for the originally significant contrast. The primary full-text source for exact outcome is the first author-uploaded penultimate manuscript at ResearchGate, cross-checked to the Guilford publisher abstract. Manipulation check did not establish increased future orientation.
replication_title: Letters to our Future Selves? High-Powered Replication Attempts Question Effects on Future Orientation, Delinquent Decisions, and Risky Investments

replication_title: Fat talk is predicted by body dissatisfaction and social comparison with no interaction effect: Evidence from two replication studies

effect_name: Prefrontal value signal and control in food choice
effect_claim: The vmPFC encodes goal values during food choice, while dlPFC activity supports successful self-control.

We found that vmPFC activity was correlated with goal values regardless of the amount of self-control and it correlated with both taste and health in self-controllers but only taste in non-self-controllers. We did not find strong support for the hypothesized role of left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) in self-control.

review_note: Independent-author conceptual retest of the Elman and McClelland lexical-compensation effect using pretested speech materials, followed by a separate within-paper direct replication. The later authors acknowledge mixed past evidence and show robust effects in two new samples.

replication_target_quote: Our experiments are based on a previous demonstration of direct-access retrieval in language processing, presented in McElree et al. (2003). Experiment 1 replicates the original result using an auditory implementation of the Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff (SAT) method.
outcome_quote: Both of our experiments demonstrate the signature pattern of direct-access retrieval: variation in accuracy based on dependency distance, but constant retrieval speed when a distal constituent is required to complete a long-distance dependency.
review_note: Independent-author auditory SAT retest in new participants. Experiment 1 explicitly targets McElree et al.; Experiment 2 extends to poor readers.

effect_name: Intrusion and avoidance of stressful memories predict depression course

replication_target_quote: We aimed to replicate and extend these investigations by exploring the role of intrusion and avoidance of intrusive memories, as well as memory characteristics, in the prediction of depression prospectively.

review_note: Independent-author six-month prospective retest with a new mixed community sample (64 followed up). effect_name: Forward versus backward digit span IQ and group patterns

effect_claim_quote: It was predicted that forward digit span (FDS) should correlate less with IQ than backward digit span (BDS), and age and race should interact with FDS-BDS, with the FDS-BDS difference decreasing as a function of age and a greater white-black difference in BDS than in FDS. replication_target_quote: In the current study we re-examine Jensen and Figueroa's results on the basis of a large, nationally representative database.

However, in contrast to the Spearman's hypothesis, we find that the Hispanic–White difference is larger in DSF than in DSB. In addition, in contrast to Jensen and Figueroa (1975), we find that within groups proxies of GMA tend to be more strongly associated with DSF than DSB.
review_note: Independent-author reanalysis of the original two digit-span predictions using a distinct nationally representative dataset. The Black-White forward/backward score-difference pattern recurred, but the within-group general-ability association reversed; a Hispanic-White extension also differed. These are descriptive sample patterns and do not establish a biological or causal group explanation.

effect_name: Relational frame training raises children's full-scale IQ
effect_claim: The 2011 pilot reported that relational frame training increased full-scale IQ in children, including an advantage over matched untreated controls in its first study.
effect_claim_quote: Matched against a no-treatment control group, experimental participants showed significant improvements in full-scale IQ following stimulus equivalence training, and a further significant rise following relational frame training.
replication_target_quote: This study aimed to replicate and extend the pilot findings of Cassidy et al. (2011) which found that teaching children to derive various relations among stimuli leads to increases in the full scale IQ scores of both typically developing children and those with educational and learning difficulties.
outcome_quote: Significant increases in full scale IQ of around one standard deviation were recorded for each child.
review_note: Cov index73. Later article explicitly identifies the 2011 Cassidy et al. pilot as the work it aims to replicate and extend. Original Study 1 treated four children with four matched untreated controls; Study 2 treated eight children with difficulties. Later Experiment 1 recruited a new class cohort of fifteen 11–12-year-olds and found full-scale IQ gains; later Experiment 2 enrolled thirty 15–17-year-olds and reported verbal/numerical reasoning gains. The full-scale IQ replication claim is scoped to later Experiment 1. Cassidy and Roche are authors on both papers; this is a shared-author, new-participant replication under the user-expanded criteria. Cached later OpenAlex W2301889832 Psychology primary.

outcome_quote: Our primary prediction was confirmed: Truth tellers provided significantly more verifiable details than liars.
review_note: Wiley original summary and later published direct-replication summary identify the exact information-protocol condition; later uses n=72 new mock-crime statements. original_title: Self-regulatory failure: a resource-depletion approach
effect_name: Emotion suppression undermines later eating restraint
effect_claim: For chronically restrained eaters, suppressing emotional expression weakens later restraint over tempting food.
effect_claim_quote: As hypothesized, exerting self-control during the first task led to decrements in self-control on a subsequent task.
replication_title: And deplete us not into temptation: Automatic attitudes, dietary restraint, and self-regulatory resources as determinants of eating behavior
replication_target_quote: Vohs and Heatherton (2000, Study 3) showed that emotion suppression undermined participants’ success in restraining their eating behavior in a subsequent ice-cream tasting task.
outcome_quote: In contrast, when self-regulation resources were low, candy consumption was primarily predicted by automatic candy attitudes, with dietary restraint standards showing a tendency for counterintentional effects.
review_note: Independent N=50 (51 recruited, one excluded) conceptual retest explicitly citing Vohs/Heatherton 2000 Study 3. Like that study, participants suppressed versus freely expressed emotion during film viewing, then tasted a tempting food; here M&Ms, with continuous restraint scale rather than preselected chronic dieters. Depletion significantly changed the restraint-consumption association, but overall candy intake was not higher (15.42g vs 17.42g) and the positive restraint slope within depletion was only a tendency (p=.10). Scoped mixed, not a general successful main effect. Original/later authors disjoint. OpenAlex W1971287708, Psychology first field in public metadata.

replication_target_quote: These results extend previous findings (Parong et al., 2017), and highlight a somewhat rare case in which playing a focused computer game for a short duration causes improvements in a targeted executive function skill.
outcome_quote: In Experiment 1, students who played Alien Game for 4 hr, mostly at home, improved shifting skill more than those who played a word-search control game (d = .40). In Experiment 2, students who played All You Can ET (an updated version of Alien Game) for 2 hr improved shifting skill more than those who played a word-search control game (d = .36)
review_note: Cov index111. Later Journal of Educational Psychology primary publisher preview on ResearchGate expressly identifies Parong et al. (2017), whose exact original is DOI 10.1016/j.cedpsych.2017.07.002, as previous evidence being extended. Original 2017 experiments trained different college-student groups for 2 h or 1 h; later 2020 article reports fresh experiments involving 4 h Alien Game and 2 h updated All You Can ET against word-search controls. Outcome is successful for targeted shifting skill, while later did not find transfer to inhibition. Parong and Mayer recur as authors; shared-author, new-participant replication under user-expanded criteria. Cached later OpenAlex W2973395501 Psychology primary.

review_note: Relinked the machine-suggested original 2016 visual-bias paper to Cornelissen et al. 2015, the actual first clinical-group comparison expressly identified by the 2024 paper. outcome_quote: Regardless of the focus of Q2, and in line with prior research, behavioral cues were reported less often, and contextual indicators more often, in responding to Q2 than in responding to Q1. However, contrary to prior findings, behavioral cues still predominated in the responses to Q2.
review_note: New survey tested whether the specific-versus-general question framing drove the original beliefs/experience difference. Relative shift toward contextual information replicated across question versions, but contextual answers did not become the majority in Q2 as in the original; therefore mixed. Jaume Masip is an author of both papers; the later participants are a new sample. Later OpenAlex primary Psychology.

replication_target_quote: In the Stroop task (Stroop, 1935), participants view words one at a time in different colors.
outcome_quote: Across the replication studies (N = 3,279), participants took longer to categorize incongruent words than congruent words
review_note: Cov index65. Many Labs 3 expressly names Stroop (1935) as the source and tests the core word-color interference with congruent versus incongruent trials. Across new multi-site participants, reaction-time interference replicated robustly (reported d=.88, t(3336)=50.22); all site estimates were significant and positive. The procedure used fewer colors and trials than Stroop's original and the paper explicitly expected a smaller effect. Original paper is 1935 with sole author Stroop, so participants and authors are disjoint. Cached later OpenAlex Psychology primary for DOI 10.1016/j.jesp.2015.10.012.

effect_name: Trait positive emotionality predicts stronger anxiety treatment response
effect_claim: Anxiety patients with higher positive emotionality before CBT or exposure therapy show greater symptom reduction during treatment.
effect_claim_quote: Participants who reported a greater propensity to experience positive emotions at pre-treatment displayed the largest reduction in anxiety symptoms as well as fewer symptoms following treatment.
replication_target_quote: we conducted a secondary analysis of an exposure therapy trial for social anxiety disorder (SAD) to examine whether individual differences in the trait-like tendency to experience positive valence emotions predicts treatment success.
outcome_quote: patients with higher pre-treatment positive emotionality displayed faster social anxiety symptom reductions and lower scores at 3-month follow-up.
review_note: Taylor et al. 2023 primary discussion explicitly compares its finding with the earlier Taylor, Knapp et al. 2017 trial (DOI 10.1016/j.brat.2017.03.006). The original is a secondary analysis of a GAD/panic-disorder CBT dataset with n=59; the later paper analyzes a different d-cycloserine augmentation trial in SAD, N=152, registration NCT02066792. Charles Taylor is shared. Both show higher pre-treatment positive emotionality predicting better treatment symptom reduction. The later trial data are new relative to the original, though this report is a secondary analysis; it does not establish a causal effect of increasing positive emotion.

original_title: Dispositional use of emotion regulation strategies and resting-state cortico-limbic functional connectivity
original_authors: Maria Picó-Pérez, Pino Alonso, Oren Contreras-Rodríguez, Ignacio Martínez-Zalacaín, Clara López-Solà, Susana Jiménez-Murcia, Antonio Verdejo-García, José M. Menchón, Carles Soriano-Mas

effect_claim: Greater dispositional cognitive reappraisal is associated with more negative resting-state connectivity between basolateral amygdala and insula or supplementary motor area.
effect_claim_quote: FC between left BLA and left insula and right BLA and the supplementary motor area (SMA) correlated inversely with reappraisal scores.
replication_target_quote: To do so, we reanalyzed own existing data (Diers et al., 2014; Scheffel et al., 2019) from three related ER experiments containing measures of dispositional use of reappraisal and suppression (via ERQ) and fMRI resting-state scans to replicate the findings by Picó-Pérez et al. (2018).
outcome_quote: we were not able to replicate a correlation of dispositional ER strategy use with functional connectivity between the amygdala and PFC regions
review_note: The Frontiers article explicitly identifies Picó-Pérez et al. 2018 DOI 10.1007/s11682-017-9762-3 as direct replication target for its first aim. Original primary abstract reports 48 healthy controls and inverse basolateral-amygdala to insula/SMA connectivity with ERQ reappraisal. Later authors preregistered hypotheses and analyzed 107 independent healthy adults from three pre-existing Dresden experiments; this is new participant data relative to the original, though a secondary analysis. Corrected primary result was null. The later authors note differing fMRI acquisition/preprocessing, a larger PFC search mask, and younger participants; exploratory uncorrected clusters were observed but do not rescue the preregistered corrected result.

original_title: Testing the mindfulness-to-meaning theory: Evidence for mindful positive emotion regulation from a reanalysis of longitudinal data

effect_name: Mindfulness training increases reappraisal through decentering and broadened awareness
effect_claim: Mindfulness training improves positive reappraisal through greater decentering and broadened awareness.
effect_claim_quote: Significant indirect effects indicated that increases in decentering mediated the effect of mindfulness training on broadening awareness, which in turn mediated enhanced reappraisal efficacy.
replication_target_quote: Central to the Mindfulness to Meaning Theory is the mindful reappraisal hypothesis (MRH), which suggests mindfulness training promotes well-being by facilitating positive reappraisal.
outcome_quote: mindfulness training increased decentering, which in turn broadened awareness, which was then associated with positive reappraisal
review_note: The 2021 report explicitly presents a replication of the mindful-reappraisal hypothesis modeled in Garland et al. 2017 DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0187727. The original analyzed a social-anxiety MBSR-versus-CBT randomized trial (N=107), while the later report analyzes a distinct six-year Norwegian MBSR-versus-no-training randomized cohort of medical/psychology students; four authors overlap. Both primary abstracts support the decentering → broader awareness → positive-reappraisal pathway. Distal outcomes differ (original positive affect, later well-being), so the effect is scoped to the reappraisal mechanism, not an identical distal outcome. Both reports are secondary/longitudinal analyses of different trial data.

effect_name: Achievement motivation predicts false autobiographical memory
effect_claim: Explicit achievement motives predicted false belief and memory inflation for suggested childhood achievement events.

replication_target_quote: Previous research (Sharman & Calacouris, 2010. Motivated imagination inflation: Implicit and explicit motives predict imagination inflation for achievement and affiliation events. Experimental Psychology, 57, 77–82) found that participants’ achievement-motivation was associated with the inflation of memory and confidence for unlikely achievement-related events in childhood.
outcome_quote: Both Experiments did not find, as earlier research had, a significant relationship between achievement-motivation and achievement-related memory distortion.
original_title: Do people's motives influence their susceptibility to imagination inflation?
replication_title: Lessons for future research: two experiments failed to reproduce a relationship between achievement motivation and autobiographical memory distortion
replication_authors: Lawrence Patihis; Paul Cloud; Kenneth Nguyen
review_note: OpenAlex W2895939656 primary Psychology, published journal article. Later institutional primary abstract cites Sharman & Calacouris (2010), Experimental Psychology 57:77–82, but gives a descriptive rather than canonical article title; PubMed resolves the exact cited authors, volume and pages to DOI 10.1027/1618-3169/a000010, titled 'Do people's motives influence their susceptibility to imagination inflation?'. Original recruited 46 UNSW undergraduates; later paper reports two new U.S. undergraduate experiments using false-feedback (rather than imagination-only) methods. Both fail the narrow original association between explicit achievement motivation and achievement-related memory inflation, although false feedback itself works and Experiment 2 reports an interaction; this is a conceptual replication of the motive association, not a direct procedural replication. Experiment 2 was preregistered according to its author manuscript.

The later article explicitly identifies this earlier efficacy study, uses a separate 30-school 2019 cluster RCT with 5,494 first/second graders, and reproduces the science vocabulary-depth effect (ES 0.50). The later study did not replicate domain-general reading comprehension; this row is deliberately restricted to the science vocabulary outcome. Later OpenAlex W3139712811 primary field Psychology.

review_note: The original article abstract reports its weapon-focus result; the later full text explicitly confirms a significant memory-related effect in Pickel and Sneyd Experiment 1. Later Experiment 3 used the unaltered videos, original questionnaire, and 266 new German participants. Gun versus phone did not impair appearance memory. The gun did attract gaze in the separate slide-show experiment, so the failure is scoped to perpetrator memory, not all attention effects. No shared authors. Official OpenAlex W4318763919 primary field Psychology.

outcome_quote: none of the interaction effects between culture and DRD4 were significant

review_note: Two fresh-participant experiments used a new athlete stimulus set. The nonacting negative compatibility pattern recurred and disappeared or reversed with skilled action; the novel context hypothesis did not succeed, but it is outside the original effect. Tipper and Bach authored both studies. Official OpenAlex W3043823709 primary field Psychology.

original_authors: Stephen J. Lupker, Manuel Perea, Colin J. Davis

replication_target_quote: The question in Experiment 2 was would the pattern reported by Lupker et al. (2008) of a sizable TL priming effect for consonants (24 ms in that article) and no TL priming effect for vowels (3 ms) replicate?
outcome_quote: The results of Experiment 2 replicated the consonant TL priming effect reported in Lupker et al.'s (2008) Experiment 1a. The results for the vowel TL priming effect (a significant 13 ms) did not.
review_note: Experiment 2 tested new participants with the exact Lupker et al. Experiment 1a stimuli. It reproduced consonant priming but found significant vowel priming, contrary to the original zero-vowel component. The later authors describe the original vowel null as likely a Type II error. Lupker authored both studies. Official OpenAlex W2990001930 primary field Psychology.

review_note: Later article explicitly describes conceptual replication of two prior MTS-PD studies, identified in the author dissertation as Gage et al. 2017 DOI 10.1177/1098300717693568 and Gage et al. 2018 DOI 10.1002/pits.22106. This row points to the earliest already-curated effect page. Original 2017 Study 2 showed emailed visual feedback increased teacher behavior-specific praise; the 2018 separate four-teacher replication is already attached. Later study enrolled four other teachers and delivered targeted training plus emailed/texted visual feedback, again observing functional relation with increased teacher praise. Three authors overlap; new teacher participants. Outcome scope is teacher praise, not student behavior. OpenAlex W3128592705 primary Psychology. Later published online 2021-02-10 (2023 issue).

effect_name: Nesbitt smoking arousal-emotional response paradox
effect_claim: Among smokers, cigarette smoking increased physiological arousal while reducing emotional response relative to simulated smoking.
effect_claim_quote: Smokers were less emotional when smoking than when simulating smoking, and with the high-nicotine cigarette than with the low-nicotine cigarette.
replication_target_quote: The present study attempted to replicate Nesbitt's Paradox.
outcome_quote: Emotional and physiological arousal showed a significant positive relationship (r = .65), contradicting Nesbitt's report of an inverse relationship.
original_title: Smoking, physiological arousal, and emotional response
replication_title: Cigarette smoking, physiological arousal, and emotional response: Nesbitt's Paradox re-examined
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
review_note: OpenAlex W2010274228 is a published article with primary field Psychology. Shiffman and Jarvik 1984 explicitly attempted to replicate Nesbitt 1973; the exact DOI is verified by PubMed and the original APA publisher preview. Nesbitt enrolled 30 smokers and 30 nonsmokers; the later paper recruited 10 smokers for new smoking and sham-smoking sessions. The later positive arousal–emotional-response association contradicted the original inverse association, and smoking did not change pain thresholds or MAACL Anxiety. Verdict failed for the narrow Nesbitt paradox effect; physiological heart-rate increase did recur.

review_note: OpenAlex W2058722003 is a published article with primary field Psychology. Wetzel, Wilson and Kort 1981 explicitly identify Nisbett and Wilson 1977, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 35:250–256; DOI is independently confirmed by the author-provided original article. Shared author Wilson participated, but the later paper reports new participants and altered forewarning and introspection conditions. The original warm-versus-cold teacher halo on appearance, mannerisms and accent recurred even after forewarning; the unawareness result also recurred. Verdict successful for the narrow halo effect. Not a claim that all halo effects generalize.

review_note: Original Arnold et al. 1993 Psychological Assessment paper identified three Parenting Scale factors in parents of young/preschool children. Prinzie et al. 2007 explicitly targeted that factor structure in a separate proportionally stratified Belgian sample of 596 mothers and 559 fathers of elementary-school children. Its confirmatory factor analysis failed the original three-factor structure; it found two interpretable laxness/overreactivity factors and reproduced these at 3-year follow-up within its own cohort. The effect row concerns the cross-study test of the 1993 three-factor result; the later internal follow-up is not an independent replication of Arnold. Authors disjoint, children older, new participants. Official OpenAlex W2129081088 primary field Psychology.

Swanson authored both. Official OpenAlex primary Psychology. Official work ID W2075249441.

original_title: Sex differences in human mate preferences: Evolutionary hypotheses tested in 37 cultures

review_note: Buss 1989 DOI 10.1017/S0140525X00023992 used 37 cultural samples, total N=10,047, and reported that women valued resource-acquisition cues in potential mates more than men. Buss 1990 DOI 10.1177/0022022190211001 describes the same historical dataset and should not be double-counted as a separate original experiment.

The later primary Elsevier page cites Nicholas Bateson's 1966 Journal of Experimental Social Psychology familiarization study in its references, and its abstract explicitly tests the earlier finding. Bateson's DOI and outcome are from the original Elsevier abstract. Teger, Pruitt, St. Jean and Haaland recruited 226 new participants across three universities and five studies; none found increased individual risk from mere familiarity. effect_name: Syllabic length slows naming of low-frequency words

The abstract of Goldiamond and Hawkins's 1958 paper is visible in its APA publisher preview reproduced on ResearchGate; it reports a logarithmic training-frequency/recognition-response relationship in blank trials. Richards's new experiment explicitly repeated Goldiamond and Hawkins with a dual-modality design and postexperiment interview. The exact scoped success quote is visible on Richards's author profile https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Larry-Richards in its entry for this paper; the full paper abstract is indexed at https://openalex.org/W2318878218. The direct ResearchGate article page is access restricted in current tools. The interview raises a separate interpretation caveat. Success refers only to the blank-trial training-frequency response pattern, not a perceptual theory. Authors are disjoint.

original_title: Instructor Mindset Beliefs and Behaviors: How Do Students and Instructors Perceive Them?
original_authors: Katherine Muenks, Kathryn M. Kroeper, Elizabeth A. Canning, Mary C. Murphy
replication_title: Growth mindset beliefs and practices among students and academic advisors: a conceptual replication of Muenks et al. (2024)
replication_authors: Darby K. Matusz, Matthew H. Kim, Jennifer Osterhage
effect_name: Perceived growth-mindset behavior predicts perceived instructor or advisor mindset
effect_claim: Students’ perceptions of instructors’ growth-mindset behaviors are strongly associated with students’ perceptions of those instructors’ growth-mindset beliefs.
effect_claim_quote: students’ perceptions of instructor behavior were indeed the strongest predictor of students’ perceptions of instructor mindset, B=0.40, p<.001.
replication_target_quote: the goal of the present study was to conduct a conceptual replication of Muenks et al. (2024), which examined associations between instructor growth mindset beliefs and behaviors and how students perceive their instructors’ beliefs and behaviors.
outcome_quote: Results closely mirrored those of the original findings in both magnitude and pattern of significance, except that the present study found a small negative association between advisors’ self-reported growth mindset beliefs and student perceptions of their advisor’s growth mindset beliefs.
review_note: Muenks et al. 2024 DOI 10.1007/s11218-024-09948-6 found, among 765 students with 44 instructors, student-perceived instructor growth-mindset behavior was the strongest predictor of student-perceived instructor mindset (B=.40, p<.001). Matusz et al. 2026 explicitly conceptually replicated the association pattern with fresh 434 students and 13 professional academic advisors at a separate university, reporting closely mirrored magnitude/significance except one distinct association: advisor self-reported belief versus student-perceived advisor belief turned slightly negative. Scope this row to student-perceived behavior→student-perceived belief, not the discordant advisor self-report association. Later abstract reports the broader result but not an individual coefficient; inference of success for the scoped path follows from its stated sole exception. Author lists disjoint. OA primary Psychology.

effect_name: Dichotic listening attention test predicts bus-driver accidents
effect_claim: Greater susceptibility to attentional disruption on a dichotic-listening test was associated with a higher road-accident rate in bus drivers.
effect_claim_quote: A measure of proneness to this type of disruption was significantly related to accident rate.
replication_target_quote: The embedded figures test (EFT) of Witkin (1950) and the dichotic listening test (DLT) of Gopher and Kahneman (1971) were chosen on the basis of previously reported correlations with driving accident rate.
outcome_quote: The DLT showed no correlations with driver performance measures, thus failing to replicate earlier findings.
original_title: Relation of a test of attention to road accidents
replication_title: Cognitive abilities and safety on the road: a re-examination of individual differences in dichotic listening and search for embedded figures
original_authors: Daniel Kahneman; Rachel Ben-Ishai; Michael Lotan
replication_authors: Frank P. McKenna; John Duncan; Ivan D. Brown
review_note: Official OpenAlex W2085636960 classifies the later 1986 journal article as primary Psychology. McKenna, Duncan, and Brown measured the Gopher-Kahneman dichotic-listening test and prospective accident outcomes in 153 new bus-driver trainees; the publisher abstract states it failed to correlate with driver-performance measures. The original source is Kahneman, Ben-Ishai, and Lotan's 1973 Journal of Applied Psychology study (DOI 10.1037/h0035426), which used the Gopher-Kahneman test in 39 professional bus drivers and reported a significant relation with accident rate. The later abstract identifies the test and prior driving-accident correlation but does not name the 1973 paper; exact linkage follows from those distinctive details and the 1973 primary paper. Scope is dichotic-listening/accident association only, not the separate embedded-figures test.

original_title: Emotion Naming Impedes Both Cognitive Reappraisal and Mindful Acceptance Strategies of Emotion Regulation
original_authors: Erik C. Nook, Ajay B. Satpute, Kevin N. Ochsner

effect_claim: Naming an emotion before using a regulation strategy makes that strategy less effective than regulating without naming.
effect_claim_quote: Participants who named their emotions before reappraising reported feeling worse than those who regulated without naming.
replication_target_quote: The current study replicated the procedures of the original emotion naming study in a new sample of younger adults (18-25 years, N=68) and older adults (60+ years, N=68).
outcome_quote: naming made people feel worse on both regulation and non-regulation trials (i.e., naming did not impede regulation exclusively).
review_note: Original experiments N80 and N60 attributed the difference to naming specifically blocking regulation. New independent younger and older samples N68 each found a general negative effect of naming, including trials without regulation, so the specific naming-by-regulation interaction did not reproduce. Authors disjoint. Official later OpenAlex W7124889867 primary Psychology.

original_title: The dark side of environmental activism
replication_title: Environmental activism, dark triad traits, and left-wing authoritarianism: A constructive replication study

effect_claim_quote: Results showed positive associations between environmental activism and Machiavellianism, narcissism, antihierarchical aggression, and anticonventionalism.
replication_target_quote: The goal of the current study was to constructively replicate this previous study with a larger sample ( N = 1998 employed individuals in Germany) and time-lagged panel data
outcome_quote: Machiavellianism and civic environmental actions positively predicted each other over time.
review_note: Original cross-sectional German employed sample N839; later new German employed sample N1998 followed over one year, supporting the specifically scoped positive Machiavellianism/civic-action link with stronger temporal evidence. Other original trait-activism links are mixed or directional, so this page names only the Machiavellianism/civic-action association. Zacher authored both, new sample disclosed. Official later OpenAlex W4415328264 primary Psychology.

original_title: The gamblers of the future? Migration from loot boxes to gambling in a longitudinal study of young adults

replication_authors: Lucas Palmer, Gabriel A. Brooks, Luke Clark
effect_name: Loot-box spending predicts gambling initiation among young adult gamers
effect_claim: Among young adults who did not gamble at baseline, higher spending on randomized loot boxes predicts starting real-money gambling six months later.
effect_claim_quote: Among baseline non-gamblers, loot box expenditure and RLI predicted gambling initiation (logistic regressions) and later gambling spending (linear regressions).
replication_target_quote: testing the replicability of results of Brooks & Clark [3] within a regional sample in Western Canada
outcome_quote: Among non-gambling participants at baseline, loot box spending and RLI predicted gambling initiation at the follow-up, in a Bayesian logistic regression with informed priors.
review_note: Original baseline subgroups: 415 non-gamblers and 221 gamblers. Later new British Columbia sample: 83 non-gamblers and 43 gamblers; 6-month follow-up and randomized-versus-direct-purchase contrast retested. Bayesian informed-prior initiation analysis supported the original; frequentist initiation estimate was less conclusive, so the page is scoped to the authors’ reported prospective Bayesian result and avoids causal language. Brooks and Clark authored both. Official later OpenAlex W4410019340 primary Psychology.

original_title: A Novel Brief Therapy for Patients Who Attempt Suicide: A 24-months Follow-Up Randomized Controlled Study of the Attempted Suicide Short Intervention Program (ASSIP)
original_authors: Anja Gysin-Maillart, Simon Schwab, Leila Maria Soravia, Millie Megert, Konrad Michel
replication_title: Randomized controlled trial for the Attempted Suicide Short Intervention Program (ASSIP): An independent non-replication study
replication_authors: Anna Monn, Tania Villar de Araujo, Annia Rüesch, Golo Kronenberg, Christoph Hörmann et al.
effect_name: ASSIP plus usual care reduces repeat suicidal behavior after an attempt
effect_claim: Adding the three-session ASSIP intervention to usual care reduces repeat suicide attempts among recent attempters.
effect_claim_quote: During the 24-month follow-up period, five repeat suicide attempts were recorded in the ASSIP group and 41 attempts in the control group.
replication_target_quote: this study re-evaluated the efficacy of a brief intervention (ASSIP - Attempted Suicide Short Intervention Program) for patients with a recent suicide attempt in reducing repeated suicidal behavior.
outcome_quote: The intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis found no significant effect of ASSIP in reducing suicidal behavior or admission to psychiatric hospitals.
review_note: Original Bern randomized trial N120 reported fewer repeat attempts over 24 months with ASSIP; independent new trial N92 followed 12 months and found no benefit on suicidal behavior in ITT, while per-protocol reattempt incidence was higher. Follow-up and composite primary outcome differ, clearly disclosed. No overlapping authors. Official later OpenAlex W4409199247 primary Psychology.

original_title: Epistemic trust and associations with psychopathology: Validation of the German version of the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity-Questionnaire (ETMCQ)
original_authors: Anna-Maria Weiland, Svenja Taubner, Max Zettl, Leonie C. Bartmann, Nina Frohn, Mirijam Luginsland, Jana Volkert
replication_title: Replicability or revision? Further evidence on the psychometric quality of the German version of the epistemic trust, mistrust and credulity questionnaire
replication_authors: Nicola-Hans Schwarzer, Noëlle Behringer, Paula Dees, Stephan Gingelmaier, Melanie Henter, Holger Kirsch, Tillmann Kreuzer, Robert Langnickel, Pierre-Carl Link, Sascha Müller, Agnes Turner, Tobias Nolte
effect_name: Good fit of the 12-item German epistemic trust questionnaire model
effect_claim: The shortened 12-item German ETMCQ factor model has good model fit, with CFI above .95; CFI/TLI above .90 count as acceptable.
effect_claim_quote: The model fit to the data was good for a shortened 12-item version.
replication_target_quote: Therefore, we prioritized an independent replication of the 12-item model proposed by Weiland et al.
outcome_quote: The 12-item adaptation yielded superior fit relative to both the unmodified 15-item model and the 15-item solution of Campbell et al. However, in our sample the Weiland model’s fit indices remained below optimal thresholds
review_note: Weiland et al. 2024 derived a 12-item German three-factor ETMCQ model with correlated residuals in N=584 general-population panel respondents. Original PDF Table 2: CFI=.96, TLI=.94, RMSEA=.054, SRMR=.043; its methods defined >.90 CFI/TLI as acceptable, >.95 as good, and abstract judged overall fit good despite TLI=.94. Schwarzer et al. 2026 explicitly and independently tested the same 12-item model in N=567 new university students. Its PDF Table 1: CFI=.93, TLI=.91, RMSEA=.05, SRMR=.05. Thus the newer data preserve acceptable fit under original >.90 CFI/TLI thresholds and the 12-item model remains better than 15-item versions, but CFI drops below the original good-fit >.95 cutoff and the later article calls its overall fit only marginally acceptable under stricter >=.95 CFI/TLI thresholds. Mixed codes that criterion-sensitive split; do not read its abstract phrase "neither...acceptable" as a failure under the original thresholds. No author overlap. July 2026 correction changes author spelling only. Official OA W7162466822 primary Psychology.

original_title: Are Keynote and Invited Speakers at State Behavior Analytic Conferences Experts on Their Presentation Topics?
original_authors: Margaret Ayres Boggs, John T. Rapp, Jennifer L. Cook, Sarah M. Richling, Raeesa Mohamed

effect_claim_quote: nearly a third did not have any publications on their presentation topic.
replication_target_quote: the current study endeavored to replicate and extend Ayres Boggs et al. (2025) and Rapp et al. (2025) by evaluating the expertise of keynote and invited speakers at ABA conferences in Canada.
outcome_quote: Results show that over a third of keynote speakers did not have any publications on their presentation topic.
review_note: Ayres Boggs et al. 2025 used Google Scholar to count topic-specific peer-reviewed publications for keynote presentations at 111 U.S. state behavior-analytic conferences (2021–2023): 22/71 keynote speakers (31%) had zero. Mohamed et al. 2026 explicitly replicated the same expertise metrics in 17 Canadian provincial conferences (2021–2023): 8/23 keynote presentations (35%) had zero topic-specific publications. Their larger combined keynote-plus-invited estimate is 51% versus 31% in the U.S., a magnitude difference not encoded in this narrowly scoped keynote effect. The observation units are distinct conference presentations in different countries despite overlapping calendar years. Authors Mohamed, Cook, Boggs, and Rapp overlap. Official cached OpenAlex primary field Psychology.

effect_name: Conception risk and Obama voting preference

effect_claim_quote: Across two studies, we found that the intention to vote for Barack Obama in the months preceding the 2008 election increased as a function of conception risk across the menstrual cycle.
replication_target_quote: the present study reassesses the claim made in Navarrete et al. (2010) Study 1, that women's voter preference for male candidates who demonstrate cues of strong genetic fitness increases across the reproductive cycle as a function of conception risk.
outcome_quote: Contrary to the original findings, conception risk did not predict greater voter support for Obama as a younger, more attractive alternative to Donald J. Trump, nor was conception risk a significant factor in other matchups we presented to participants.
